title: Why a sprout leans toward the light
description: Put a seedling on a windowsill and within days it bends toward the glass. The plant is not deciding anything — it is growing unevenly, on purpose, steered by light itself.

body.heading: Growth that bends
paragraphs: A shoot tip senses the direction of light. In response, a growth chemical called auxin gathers on the shaded side of the stem. Auxin makes stem cells lengthen faster, so the shaded side grows more than the lit side — and the shoot curves toward the light. This response is called phototropism.
The bend is not the plant leaning like a person; it is new growth laid down unevenly. Straighten the pot around and the tip will curve back the other way within days.

body.heading: Why it is worth the effort
paragraphs: Leaves are solar panels: a shoot that finds light can feed itself, while one stuck in shade starves slowly. Bending toward brightness is how a seedling escapes the shadow of the plants around it.
Gardeners use the same trick in reverse — turning windowsill pots a quarter-turn every few days so the plant grows straight instead of lopsided.

takeaway: A sprout bends toward light because a growth chemical gathers on its shaded side and makes that side grow faster — phototropism.
